LESSON PLAN 1: ORAL LANGUAGE – TALKING ABOUT ONESELF AND
 ONE’S FAMILY

   I. OBJECTIVES

 At the end of the 45-minute lesson, the students will be able to:

         1. Share at least 3 key details about oneself (name, age, favorite

            activity) using clear voice and proper pronunciation;

         2. Talk about 2-3 family members and one thing they like to do

            together;

         3. Maintain eye contact with their audience when speaking.

   II. SUBJECT MATTER

       Topic:  Sharing  Information  About  Oneself  and  One’s  Family

       References: Adapted from elementary oral communication curricula

       and early childhood language development resources

       Materials: Visual aid (chart) with sentence starters:
     "My name is…", "I am     years old…",
      "My family has…", "We like to…"
        Picture cards (e.g., of a child, parents, siblings, toys, activities like playing, eating)
       "About Me" worksheet (simple, with spaces for drawing and writing key details)
       Evaluation checklist
  III. PROCEDURE
  1. PREPARATORY ACTIVITIES

      Warm-Up

            Lead a "Hello Circle" – students stand in a circle, take turns

       saying "Hello, my name is [name]" while waving to the class.

       Encourage them to speak loudly enough for everyone to hear.
                                                            40

     Motivation

         Show a colorful picture of a happy family doing an activity (e.g.,

      picnicking). Ask: "Who do you see in this picture?" and "What do you

       like to do with your own family?" Let 2-3 students share a quick

      thought to get them excited to talk more.





2. DEVELOPMENTAL ACTIVITIES

           Introduce Key Details: Display the visual aid with sentence

       starters. Explain that when we talk about ourselves and our family, we

     can use these sentences to make our ideas clear.

           Modeling: Share your own example in simple terms: "Hi, my name

        is [Teacher’s Name]. I am [age]. My favorite activity is reading. My family

      has [2 people] – my mom and dad. We like to cook together on

     weekends!" Use picture cards to point to each detail as you speak.

            Practice Sentence Starters: Have the class repeat the sentence

       starters together 2-3 times to build confidence.

3. GUIDED PRACTICE

           Pair-and-Share Activity: Divide students into pairs. Give each

      pair a set of picture cards to use as clues.

             1. Student A uses  the  sentence  starters  to  share  about

              themselves and their family.
                                                             41



             2. Student B listens, then shares their own information.

             3. Circulate around  pairs  to  support: remind them  to speak

              clearly, make eye contact, and use the picture cards if they get

             stuck.

            After 8 minutes, ask 2-3 volunteer pairs to share one thing they

            learned about each other with the class.

IV. EVALUATION

Use an informal checklist to assess each student during pair-and-share:


 1              2              3              4
 Pupil  mentioned Pupil mentioned  Pupil mentioned  Pupil mentioned
  only his name   2  –  3   details  4  details  about  5 or more details
                   about himself      himself           about himself

V. AGREEMENT


For homework, students will:

     Talk to one family member about their favorite activity.

     Draw a picture of themselves and that family member doing that

activity.

    Be ready to share what they learned with the class in our next lesson.

LESSON PLAN 2: ORAL LANGUAGE – FOLLOWING 1-TO-2-STEP ORAL
DIRECTIONS

I. OBJECTIVES
At the end of the 45-minute lesson, the students will be able to:

       1. Listen carefully to follow 1-step and 2-step oral directions accurately;

       2. Repeat the directions in their own words before completing them;

       3. Perform the actions in the correct order.

II. SUBJECT MATTER

      Topic: Following 1-to-2-Step Oral Directions

      References: Adapted from elementary  oral language  curricula and

     motor skill development resources

      Materials: Visual aid (chart) with action words and pictures:
      go, close, run, pick up, sit, give Simple props
      (classroom items): door, chair, book, pencil, toy
      "Mission Card" set (with pre-written 1-2 step directions) Informal
      evaluation checklist
III. PROCEDURE
1. PREPARATORY ACTIVITIES

     Warm-Up (5 minutes):

               Lead the class in an "Action Song" (e.g., "Head, Shoulders,

           Knees, and Toes") – have them follow along with your oral cues to

             practice listening and moving.

     Motivation (5 minutes):

                 Say: "Today, you’re all secret agents on a special mission!

         To complete the mission, you need to listen very carefully to my

             directions. If you follow them right, you’ll get a ‘Secret Agent

          Badge’ at the end!" Show a fun, hand-drawn badge to build

            excitement.
                                                              43


     2. DEVELOPMENTAL ACTIVITIES

                Introduce 1-Step Directions: Display the visual aid with action

          words. Give a simple 1-step direction (e.g., "Go to the chair") and do it

           yourself to model. Ask 3-4 students to try one at a time, reminding them

           to listen first.

                Introduce 2-Step Directions: Explain that 2-step directions have

         two actions to do in order. Model with: "Go to the door, then close it."

           Point to the visual cards for "go" and "close" as you speak. Have

           students repeat the direction back to you before trying it.

                 Practice Repeating Directions: Teach them the phrase, "Let me

          say  that  back:  [repeat  direction]"  to make  sure  they  understand.

           Practice with 2-3 more 2-step directions (e.g., "Pick up the book, then

          give it to me").
     3. ANALYSIS / DISCUSSION (5 minutes)
 Ask: "When I said ‘Go to the door and close it,’ what was the first thing  you did?
    The second thing?" (Let students share to confirm order.)
 Follow up: "Why is it important to listen to all the direction before you start?" (e.g.,

        "So, you don’t forget the second step," "So, you do it right")

Remind them: "Repeating the direction back helps you make sure you heard it

                                  correctly!"ss


     4. GUIDED PRACTICE (10 minutes)

                 Secret Agent Mission Trail: Set up 3 simple stations around the

          classroom. Give each small group (4-5 students) a "Mission Card" with

          a 1 or 2-step direction for each station.

                 Station 1: "Go to the window and tap it twice."

                 Station 2: "Pick up one pencil and put it on the table."

                 Station 3: "Run to the whiteboard, then sit down in your chair."

             Each student takes a turn leading their group through a station:

          they read the mission card aloud, their group repeats  it back, then

         everyone does the action together. Circulate to support and remind

          students      to     follow     order    and     speak      clearly
                                                            44


IV. EVALUATION (5 minutes)

     Give 1-2 steps directions orally. Rate the learner’s performance based
on the rubrics.

Rubrics

 1              2              3              4
 Pupil attempted  Pupil  executed  Pupil   executed   Pupil executed
 to do what has  wrongly   what  incompletely       accurately what
 been said.        has been said.    what has been     has been said.
                                       said



V. AGREEMENT
     For homework, students will:

     Be a "family helper" by following one 2-step direction from a parent or

      guardian (e.g., "Set one plate on the table and put a fork next to it").

     Ask their family member to give them a "thumbs up" if they did it right.

      Share what direction they followed with the class in our next lesson.

LESSON PLAN 3: ORAL LANGUAGE – GIVING AND FOLLOWING 1-TO-2-
         STEP ORAL DIRECTIONS IN DAILY SITUATIONS

I. OBJECTIVE
          At the end of the 45-minute lesson, the students will be able to:

       1. Give clear 1-2 step oral directions using polite language (e.g., "can

         you," "please");

       2. Follow 1-2 step directions given by a peer;

       3. Identify 2 key elements of effective directions (clarity, order) and

       polite communication.

II. SUBJECT MATTER

     Topic: Giving and Following 1-2-Step Directions (e.g., Asking a Sibling

      to Tidy Up Toys)

      References: Adapted from elementary oral communication curricula

     and social skills development resources
                                                             45


      Materials:

            Visual aid (chart) with:

             Polite phrase starters: "Can you…?", "Please…", "Thank you!"

           Action words with pictures: keep away, put in, pick up, close

         Toy props (dolls, cars, blocks, a toy box)

           Scenario cards (e.g., "Your younger sister left toys on the floor",

          "Your brother left books on the couch")

           Informal evaluation checklist
III. PROCEDURE

1. PREPARATORY ACTIVITIES

     Warm-Up (5 minutes):

          Lead a "Follow My Lead" game: Give 1-2 step directions (e.g., "Pick

     up one block and put  it on your desk") and have the class do them

       together. This review following directions before moving to giving them.

      Motivation (5 minutes):

         Show a photo of a messy playroom with toys scattered. Ask: "Have

     you ever seen a room like this? If your younger sister made this mess,

     what would you say to ask her to clean it up?" Let 2-3 students share

      quick ideas, then say: "Today, we’ll learn to ask nicely with clear steps

      so she knows exactly what to do!"





2. DEVELOPMENTAL ACTIVITIES (15 minutes)

            Introduce Polite Directions: Display the visual aid with polite

      phrases. Explain that when asking someone to do something, we use

      kind words like "can you" and "please" to be respectful.
                                                              46



          Model Giving 2-Step Directions: Use the toy props to act out the
       scenario: "Let’s pretend this doll is my younger sister, and these

     toys are on the floor. I’ll say: “‘Can you please keep your toys

    away and put them in the toy box?’" Point to the action pictures

      ("keep away," "put in") as you speak to show order.

            Practice Making Directions: Have the class repeat the model

      direction together. Then, guide them to make their own 2-step direction

      for the same scenario (e.g., "Can you pick up your cars and put them

     on the shelf?").





3. ANALYSIS / DISCUSSION

           Ask: "What polite words did I use when asking my sister?" (Let

      students point to the visual aid.)

           Follow up: "What was the first step I asked her to do? The second

      step? Why is order important?" (e.g., "So, she doesn’t get confused,"

      "So, she does everything needed").

           Ask: "How do you think your sister would feel if you asked nicely

       vs. yelling?" (Emphasize that polite language helps others want to help.)

4. GUIDED PRACTICE

           Role-Play Activity: Divide students into pairs. Give each pair a

      scenario card and toy props.

             1. One student plays the "older sibling" and gives a clear 2-step

      direction using polite language.

             2. The other student plays the "younger sibling,"  listens, and

      follows the directions.

             3. Pairs switch roles after 5 minutes.
                                                             47


      Circulate around pairs to support: Remind them to use polite phrases,

     keep directions clear, and follow steps in order. Example scenario

     prompt for pairs: "Your younger sister left her dolls on the bed. What 2

      things will you ask her to do?"


IV. EVALUATION
     Use an informal checklist to assess each student during the role-play:


                Uses polite       Gives clear        Listens
                 language (can     2-step directions   carefully and
      Criteria     you, please)       in the correct      follows peer’s
              when giving      order              directions
                   directions                           accurately
 Excellent
 Good
 Satisfactory

Note: Assess by observing each pair once. Give positive feedback like, "Great
job asking nicely!" or "Perfect order of steps!"

V. AGREEMENT
     For homework, students will:

          Find a time to give one 2-step direction to a family member

       (sibling, parent, or grandparent) using polite language (e.g., "Can you

      please pass the spoon and put it on my plate?").

         Ask the family member if they understood the directions.

      Share what direction they gave and how it went with the class in our

      next lesson.

LESSON PLAN 4: ORAL LANGUAGE – USING DESCRIBING WORDS FOR
PEOPLE, OBJECTS, THINGS, AND PLACES

I. OBJECTIVE
     At the end of the 45-minute lesson, the students will be able to:

       1. Use describing words to talk about people, objects, things, and

          places. (color, shape, size, height, weight, length, distance, etc.)

       2. Match describing words to the attributes of what they are talking

         about.

II. SUBJECT MATTER

     Topic: Recognizing and Using Describing Words (Attributes: Color,

            Shape, Size, Height, Weight, Length, Distance)

      References: Adapted from elementary oral language curricula

               and vocabulary development resources

      Materials:

            Visual aid (chart) titled "My Describing Word Toolkit" – with words

          and pictures: red, round, big, tall, heavy, long, far, cozy

           Props with different attributes: colored blocks, toys (ball, box, car,

              doll), books (thick, thin), plants  (tall, short), photos of places

           (sunny park, quiet room)

            "Describe It!" cards (with pictures of people, objects, or places)

            Informal evaluation checklist
III. PROCEDURE

1. PREPARATORY ACTIVITIES
     Warm-Up (5 minutes):

               Lead a "Word Clue" game: Say, "I’m thinking of something

             in this room that’s red. Can you guess what it is?" Have students

              call out guesses, then reveal the object. Repeat with 3-4 more

            clues (e.g., "It’s round," "It’s big").
                                                            49

     Motivation (5 minutes):
             Show a plain drawing of a cat and a colorful, detailed

           drawing of the same cat. Ask: "Which drawing tells you more

           about  the  cat? Why?"  Explain:  "Today,  we’ll  learn  about

            ‘describing words’ – these are like magic clues that help us tell

            others exactly what something looks like, feels like, or where it

               is!"





2. DEVELOPMENTAL ACTIVITIES

            Introduce Describing Words: Display  the "Describing Word

      Toolkit" chart. Point to each word and its picture, and say: "These words

      describe attributes – what something is like. ‘Red’ is a color, ‘round’ is

      a shape, ‘big’ is a size, and ‘far’ is a distance." Have students repeat

     each word aloud.

      Describing words toolkit (see intervention materials)

      1. Colors

           Red, blue, green, yellow, orange, purple, pink, black, white,

     brown

      2. Sizes

            Big, small, tall, short, long, tiny, huge

      3. Shapes

          Round, square, triangle, circle, flat
                                                             50


      4. How things feel

             Soft, hard, smooth, rough, sticky, fuzzy, warm, cold

      5. How things look

             Bright, dark, shiny, dull, clean, dirty, wet, dry

      6. Feelings (for people/animals)

          Happy, sad, angry, scared, excited, sleepy, friendly

      7. Numbers  (to describe how many)

          One, two, three, many, few, some


         Model Using Describing Words: Pick up a red, round ball and

      say: "This is a red, round ball. It’s also small enough to hold in my

      hand." Then point to a tall plant: "This is a tall, green plant that’s near

      the window." Model for a person too: "My friend Lila has curly, brown

      hair and she is happy today."

            Practice Naming Attributes: Hold up different props (e.g., thick

     book, heavy toy car) and ask: "What describing words can we use for

      this?" Have students share ideas and match them to the chart.

3. ANALYSIS / DISCUSSION

           Ask: "Why do we use describing words when we talk?" (Let

      students share: "So others can picture what we’re talking about," "To

     be clear," "To make stories more fun").

           Follow up: "Can we use more than one describing word for

     something? Let’s try with the box –  is  it square, blue, or both?"

     (Emphasize that we can combine words to give more details).

           Ask: "What describing words can we use for places, like a park?"

       (e.g., "sunny," "big," "busy").
                                                           51

    4. GUIDED PRACTICE


           "Describe It! Share It!" Activity: Divide students into pairs. Give

     each pair a "Describe It!" card with a picture (e.g., a cozy bedroom, a

      small yellow bird, a tall boy).

             1. One student looks at the picture and thinks of 2-3 describing

     words for it.

             2. They say the describing words aloud (e.g., "It’s cozy, quiet, and

      has a big bed") and their partner guesses what’s in the picture.

             3. Pairs switch roles after 5 minutes.

            Circulate to support: Remind students to use words from the

      toolkit and match them to the picture’s attributes.


IV. EVALUATION

          Use an informal checklist to assess each student during the pair

       activity:

                   Recognizes   Uses describing      Matches
                and names at words to talk about   describing
          Criteria    least 4        people/objects/places words to the
                    describing                           correct
                  words                               attributes
       Excellent

      Good

       Satisfactory


Note: Assess by listening to each pair’s descriptions. Give positive feedback

like, "Great use of ‘cozy’ for the bedroom!" or "Perfect – ‘tall’ matches the boy!"

V. AGREEMENT

For homework, students will:
        1. Pick one thing at home (a toy, a pet, a room) and think of 3 describing

     words for it.

        2. Tell a family member about it using those words (e.g., "My dog is

     brown, fluffy, and small").

Be ready to share their description with the class in our next lesson.

LESSON PLAN 5: ORAL LANGUAGE – TALKING ABOUT TOPICS OF
              INTEREST THROUGH PICTURE DISCUSSION


I. OBJECTIVE

At the end of the 45-minute lesson, the students will be able to:

      1. Share their thoughts, feelings, and observations about a picture on

         a topic of interest;

      2. Use simple sentence starters to organize their ideas clearly;

      3. Listen  respectfully  to  peers’  thoughts and  ask one  follow-up

         question.

II. SUBJECT MATTER

      Topic: Talking About Topics of Interest (e.g., Toys, Pets, Parks, Festivals)

       "Tell Me What You Think About This Picture"

      References: Adapted from elementary oral communication curricula

     and expressive language development resources

      Materials:

      Visual aid  (chart) with sentence  starters:  "I see…",  "I think…",  "I

      like…", "It makes me feel…"

      Colorful pictures of kid-friendly topics (e.g., a dog playing in a park, a

      birthday party with toys, a colorful festival, a cozy pet corner)

      "Picture Card Packs" (one pack per small group, with 3-4 pictures on

       different interests) informal evaluation checklist.

1. PREPARATORY ACTIVITIES

     Warm-Up

          Lead a "Quick Share" circle: Ask students to say one sentence

      about something they love (e.g., "I love my cat" or "I love playing with

      blocks"). Encourage them to speak clearly and look at the class.

      valuation checklist
                                                             53


     Motivation

          Hold up a bright picture of a dog playing in a sunny park. Ask:

    "Who likes dogs? What do you see in this picture? What do you think

      the dog is feeling?" Let 2-3 students call out quick ideas, then say:

     "Today, we’ll learn to share our thoughts about pictures we like – and

      hear what our friends think too!"

2. DEVELOPMENTAL ACTIVITIES

            Introduce  Picture  Discussion:  Display  the  visual  aid  with

      sentence  starters. Explain: "When we  talk about a  picture,  these

      sentences help us share what’s in our minds clearly. ‘I see’ tells what’s

      in the picture, ‘I think’ tells our ideas, and ‘I like’ tells what we enjoy

      about it."

          Model Sharing Thoughts: Focus on the dog park picture and

      share your own ideas: "I see a brown dog running with a red ball. I think

      the dog is happy because it’s playing in the sun. I like this picture

      because it makes me want to go to the park too!" Point to each sentence

       starter on the chart as you speak.

            Practice Sentence Starters: Have the class repeat the sentence

       starters together. Then, guide them to share one thought about the dog

      picture using one of the starters (e.g., "I see green grass" or "It makes

    me feel happy").
3. ANALYSIS / DISCUSSION

          Ask: "What did I do to help you understand my thoughts about

      the picture?" (Let students point to the sentence starters.)

           Follow up: "Why is it fun to talk about pictures we like?" (e.g.,

     "Because we can share what we love," "We can learn what our friends

       like too").

          Remind them: "When others are talking, we listen carefully –

       that’s how we show we care about their ideas. We can even ask a small

      question, like ‘Why do you like that?’ to learn more!"

LESSON PLAN 6: ORAL LANGUAGE – DESCRIBE AND DRAW

I. OBJECTIVE

At the end of the 45-minute lesson, the students will be able to:

      1. Use specific describing words (color, shape, size, position) to clearly

         describe a picture;

      2. Listen carefully to a peer’s description and draw what they hear;

      3. Identify 2-3 key details that make a description easy to understand.
II. SUBJECT MATTER

      Topic: "Describe and Draw" – Using Oral Language to Share Visual

              Details

      References: Adapted from elementary oral communication curricula

     and expressive/receptive language development resources

      Materials:

     Teacher’s model picture (colorful, with clear details: e.g., a red

      bird on a green tree branch next to a yellow flower)

      Set of "secret pictures" (one per pair, different from each other, with

      simple, distinct elements)

      Paper and crayons for each student
      Visual aid (chart) with key describing words: color words, round, square,

       big, small, on top, next to, under

      Informal evaluation checklist

III. PROCEDURE

1. PREPARATORY ACTIVITIES
     Warm-Up
          Lead  a "Quick Draw" game:  Say, "I’m going  to  describe

     something—draw what you hear!" Describe a simple object (e.g., "a

      small, blue square") and have students draw  it. Show their drawings

     and talk about how clear words helped them.
     Motivation

          Hold up your model picture (but don’t show it to the class yet).

      Say: "I have a secret picture! If I describe it well enough, you’ll be able

      to draw  it without even seeing  it. Want to try? Today, we’ll play a

      ‘Describe and Draw’ game where we’re like ‘picture messengers’—using

     words to send images to our friends!"
                                                            56


2. DEVELOPMENTAL ACTIVITIES
            Introduce Key  Description  Details:  Display  the  visual  aid.

      Explain: "When we describe a picture, we need to share details like what

      color things are, what shape they are, how big they are, and where they

       are. These details help the person drawing know exactly what to put on

       their paper."

           Teacher Modeling: Show the model picture to the class for 10

      seconds, then hide it. Describe it slowly and clearly: "First, there’s a big,

      green tree branch in the middle. On top of the branch, there’s a small,

      red bird with a yellow beak. Next to the bird, there’s a bright yellow

      flower with five petals. The sky behind is light blue." As you describe,

      point to the words on the visual aid. Have students draw along as you

      speak.

          Check and Discuss: Show  the model  picture again and  let

      students compare their drawings. Ask: "What details helped you draw

         it right?" (e.g., "‘on top’ told me where the bird was," "‘red’ told me its

       color").
3. ANALYSIS / DISCUSSION

           Ask: "What would happen if I forgot to say ‘small’ about the bird?

     Or ‘next to the bird’ about the flower?" (Let students share: "I might

     draw a big bird," "I might put the flower somewhere else").

           Follow up: "Why is it important to describe things in order (e.g.,

        ‘first the branch, then the bird’)?" (e.g., "So the drawer knows what to

     draw first," "It’s easier to follow").

          Remind students: "As a describer, your job is to be clear. As a

      drawer, your job is to listen closely—no peeking at the picture!"

4. GUIDED PRACTICE

             Pair "Describe and Draw" Activity: Divide students into pairs.

     Give one student in each pair a "secret picture" (they must not show it
                                                            57

      to their partner). Assign roles: Describer (has the picture) and Drawer

       (listens and draws).

II. SUBJECT MATTER

      Topic: Oral Language Development through Picture Talk

       Activities: "See & Say," "Picture Question Circle," "My Connection

      Share"

      Materials:
          1 large, colorful, detailed picture (e.g., a group of children

            playing at a park with slides, swings, trees, a dog, and ice

          cream vendor)

           Smaller copies of the same picture for each group (optional)

           Whiteboard or chart paper Marker

           "Question Cards" (with who/what/where/when/why written on

           them)

              Skills: Speaking, listening, observing, questioning

           Values Integration: Sharing, active listening, appreciating

             others’ experiences

III.  . LEARNING PROCEDURE

      A. MOTIVATION

           "Mystery Picture Peek:" Hold up the large picture with most of it

      covered, showing only a small part (e.g., the dog’s tail).

           Ask: "What do you think this is? What do you think is in the

       rest of the picture?"

           Let 3-4 students guess, then reveal the full picture with a big

      "ta-da!" to build excitement.
                                                        65



B. LESSON PROPER
1. ACTIVITY 1: SEE & SAY

Display the large picture prominently.

Explain: "Let’s play 'See & Say'! Look closely at the picture, and when

you see something, stand up and say what it is. For example: 'I see a

slide!'"

Let students take turns sharing what they notice. As they speak, write

key words on the board (e.g., children, park, slide, dog, ice cream).

Encourage more details: "Great! What color is the slide?" or "How

many children do you see?"

Check-in: Point to words on the board and ask students to point to

the corresponding item in the picture.

2. ACTIVITY 2: PICTURE QUESTION CIRCLE

Have students sit in a large circle.

Give out the 5 "Question Cards" to 5 different students.

Instructions:

1. The student with the "who" card asks: "Who is in the picture?"

  Let 2-3 students answer.

2. Pass the card to the next person, then the "what" card holder

   asks: "What are the children doing?"

3. Continue with "where" ("Where are they?"), "when" ("When do you

   think this is happening?"), and "why" ("Why do you think they’re

   happy?").

Model how to ask questions clearly and how to listen before

answering. For shy students, offer sentence starters: "I think they’re

at..." or "Maybe it’s because..."


3. ACTIVITY 3: "MY CONNECTION SHARE"

Explain: "Now, think about a time you did something like what’s in

the picture. Can you share 1 or 2 sentences about it?"
                                                           66

     Model with your own connection: "I remember going to the park with

    my friend. We played on the swings and ate ice cream!"

     Let students share in pairs first (to build confidence), then invite 4-5

      pairs to share their connections with the class. Praise all

      contributions: "That’s a wonderful story! I’m glad you had fun at the

     park too."
C. GENERALIZATION

      Gather students back together and ask: "What did we learn today

      about pictures?" (Expected answers: "Pictures have many things to

      see," "We can ask questions about them," "We can tell stories about

      our own lives from them.")

     Conclude: "Pictures are like secret doors to talking and sharing

       stories. You can use any picture to practice speaking!"

IV. EVALUATION
     Formative Assessment: Ask each student to say one thing they

     saw in the picture or one connection they made. Use a simple

     smiley face checklist to record if they spoke clearly and

      participated
V. ASSIGNMENT

     At home, find a picture in a book or on a calendar. Tell your family 3

      things you see in it and one time you did something similar. Be ready

      to share with the class tomorrow!

(For teacher’s use only: Note which students struggled with

questioning/sharing connections, which parts of the picture sparked the

most discussion, and adjustments for future lessons.)

Through Poems"


I. OBJECTIVES

By the end of the lesson, students will be able to:

      1. Recite a short, familiar poem or nursery rhyme with a clear, loud

            voice.

      2. Match their tone (happy, silly, soft) to the poem’s feeling.

      3. Use simple gestures or actions to go with key words in the poem.

      4. Listen respectfully to peers’ recitations and give a positive "thumbs

      Picture Poem Pack: Short, colorful poems/nursery rhymes with big

     "quack" for ducks, "twinkle" chimes).

      Visual "Smile & Shine Recitation”

      Checklist" (with emojis: 🗣️ = clear voice, 😊 = happy tone, ✋ =

       hats) for performances.

    A "Shining Star" sticker for each student.

III. PROCEDURE
      A. Warm-Up: "Rhyme & Clap Dance"
        Gather students in a circle.

       The teacher says a rhyming word pair (e.g., "cat – hat") and

         claps twice. Students repeat the words and clap back.

       Add simple dances: "dog – frog" → jump like a frog; "bird – word" →

          flap wings.

        Goal: Get them moving, practicing rhymes, and using their voices

          confidently.

B. Motivation
                  The Itsy-Bitsy Spider

                        by Anonymous

             Itsy bitsy spider

          climbed up the waterspout.

         down came the rain

          and washed the spider out;

           out came the sun

          and dried up all the rain;

          and the itsy-bitsy spider

          climbed up the spout again.


   Hold up a picture poem book, "The Itsy-Bitsy Spider" and point

   to the images.

  Ask: "Who knows this poem? What does the spider do?"

  Play a 1-minute audio clip of the poem with a silly, wiggly voice and

   "How did the voice sound? Was it happy? Silly?"

Explain: "Today, we’ll pick a poem, practice saying it with our best

voice, and add dances – just like the audio!"

Main Activity: "My Turn to Recite!" (15 minutes)

Break into 3 simple, hands-on steps:

      Step 1: Pick & Explore (5 minutes)

Lay out the Picture Poem Pack on tables. Students choose a poem

they know or like (based on the pictures).

The teacher helps each student point to the words as they say the

poem aloud once (to practice reading along with their voice).

Example: A student picks "Five Little Ducks" and points to each duck

as they count down.

Pair students up (buddy up a confident reciter with a quieter one).

LESSON PLAN 10: TALK, PLAY & SHARE – LITTLE VOICES
CONNECTING

Communicative Language Teaching (CLT) Strategy


I. OBJECTIVES

By the end of the lesson, students will be able to:

       1. Greet peers and ask simple questions (e.g., "What’s your name?"

         "What do you have?").

        2. Share personal information about a favorite toy (e.g., "This is my

          teddy. He’s soft.").

      4. Collaborate with a friend to create a short, simple "toy story" using

        spoken words.

      5. Listen respectfully to peers and respond with a simple comment

            (e.g., "Cool!" "I like it too!").

II. MATERIAL

      Stuffed toys or toy pictures (one per student; or let students bring

       their own favorite toy).

      "Talking Flashcards" with simple questions/responses (e.g., 🗣️

      "What’s this?" → 🗣️ "It’s a...").

    A "Chat Box" with small items (toy car, doll, ball) for picking prompts.

      Visual "Talk & Connect Checklist" (emojis: 👋 = greet, ❓ = ask, 💬 =

       share, 👂 = listen).

      "Friendship Sticker" for each student.
III. PROCEDURE

    1. Preparatory Activities

   A. Warm-Up/Motivation: "Hello, Friend! Circle" (5 minutes)

      Gather students in a circle.

     The teacher models: "Hi! My name is [Teacher’s name]. How are you,

      [Student’s name]?"
                                                          71


   Students take turns greeting the friend next to them, using the same

    pattern. Add a fun twist: they can wave, high-five, or do a silly dance

   while greeting.

   Goal: Practice real, face-to-face interaction and basic greetings.
 2. Developmental Activities

   Introduction: "Our Toys, Our Stories" (5 minutes)

   Hold up a stuffed toy and say: "This is my bunny. Her name is Floppy.

   She likes to jump!"

   Ask: "Who has a toy at home? What’s your toy like?" Let 2–3 students

   share quickly.
3. Analysis/Discussion

   Explain: "Today, we’ll talk to our friends about our toys—ask them

   questions, share stories, and play together with words!"

  Show the Talk & Connect Checklist and point to each emoji: "These

   are our super skills for talking today!"
4. Guided Practice

   Main Activity: "Chat & Play Stations"

   Divide students into 3 small groups. Rotate stations every 5 minutes

   (keep it fast-paced for little attention spans!).

    Station 1: "Toy Show & Tell Chat"

   Task: Students take turns showing their toy (or picture) and sharing

   1–2 things about it (e.g., "This is my car. It goes ‘vroom!’").

         Peer Interaction: After each share, friends ask a simple question

   (using flashcards as a guide): "What color is it?" or "Do you like it?"

  Why it’s CLT: Real sharing and question-asking about personal

    things.

   Station 2: "Find a Toy Match"

        Task: Students walk around the station with their toy/picture.

   They ask each other: "Do you have a [car/doll/teddy]?"

   Goal: Find a friend with the same type of toy. Once they match, they

   high-five and say: "We both have a [toy]!"

  Why it’s CLT: Real-world "searching and matching" conversation.
                                                            72

      Station 3: "Make a Toy Story Together"

     Task: Pairs pick a toy from the Chat Box. They create a 2-sentence

      story together (e.g., "This is a ball. The ball bounces to the dog!").

           Bonus: Add simple actions (bounce like a ball, bark like a dog)

      while saying the story.

    Why it’s CLT: Collaborative communication to create something

      meaningful.
            Closure: "Share Our Toy Stories" (5 minutes)
            Invite 3–4 pairs to share their short toy story with the class.

      After each story, the class responds with a positive comment: "That’s

      funny!" or "I love your ball! “Ask 1–2 students: "What was fun about

      talking to your friend today?" (e.g., "I found a friend with a teddy

       too!").

     End with a class cheer: "Talk, play, share—we’re great at caring and

      sharing!"

     Give every student a "Friendship Sticker" for using their talking skills.
IV. EVALUATION

     Use the visual Talk & Connect Checklist to observe:

            Greets peers appropriately.

          Asks simple questions.

           Shares ideas clearly (even if words are simple).

            Listens when others talk.

     Note how students interact—do they take turns? Do they respond to

       their friends’ words?

    No formal testing—focus on participation and effort to communicate.

    LESSON PLAN 11: ORAL LANGUAGE – WORD FRIENDS (WORD
                        ASSOCIATION)

I. OBJECTIVE

     At the end of the lesson, the pupils are expected to:

             1. Think of words that go together (e.g., “cat” → “milk,” “paws,”

              “meow”).

             2. Find 3 ways words connect: same meaning, opposites, or

               things that go together.

             3. Share their word friends and explain why they connect.

II. SUBJECT MATTER

      Topic: Word Friends (How Words Connect)

      Materials:

          Big pictures (cat, cake, park, sun).

         Toy props (toy cat, ball, small umbrella).

           Smiley face stickers.

           Simple chart with examples:

         Same meaning: “happy” → “glad.”

            Opposites: “big” → “small.”

           Things that go together: “bread” → “butter.”
 III. PROCEDURE

      1. Warm-Up: “Word Catch!” (5 minutes)

         Game: Toss a soft ball.

           Teacher says a word (e.g., “red”).

           Student catches the ball and says a word friend (e.g., “apple”).

            Class claps if it makes sense!
      2. Motivation: “Guess My Word Friend!” (5 minutes)

          Hold up a toy cat.

           Ask: “What words do you think of?

         Meow? Milk? Paws?”

            Say: “Today, we’ll play with word friends—words that love to go

             together!”
                                                            74


      3. Activity 1: “Word Friends on the Board” (10 minutes)

           Step 1: Stick a picture of a cat on the board.

           Ask: “What words go with cat?” Students shout out (e.g., “milk,”

              “tail”). Add their words with sticky notes.

           Step 2: Show how words connect:

                 “Milk” → goes with cat.
                  “Small” → opposite of big.

               “Happy” → same as glad.
      4. Activity 2: “Word Chain Game” (10 minutes)

          Groups of 4: Sit in circles.

           Teacher gives a starting word (e.g., “sun”).

          Each student adds a word friend (e.g., “sun” → “hot” → “ice

              cream” → “sprinkles”).

     Use props (e.g., toy umbrella for “rain”) to help them think!
      5. Wrap-Up: “Why Word Friends?” (5 minutes)

           Ask:

         “Why is ‘cat’ friends with ‘milk’?” (They go together!)

        “How do word friends help us talk?” (They make stories fun!)

            Sticker Time: Give everyone a smiley sticker for participating!

IV. EVALUATION

      Observe:

          Did the student share a word friend?

          Did they try to explain the connection (even with gestures)?

           Symbols:

      🌟 = Shared 3+ words and explained.

     👍 = Shared 1-2 words.

      😊 = Tried their best!

V. HOMEWORK

      1. Draw & Tell: Draw a cat or sun and tell your family 2-word friends.

      2. Bring a Prop: Bring a small toy or picture of their favorite word

         friend for show-and-tell next class.
                                                            75


    TEACHER TIPS

     Use actions (e.g., meowing for “cat”) to help explain connections.
     Keep it silly! If a student says “cat → spaceship,” ask, “Why?” and

     laugh together.

      Sing a goodbye song: “Bye-bye, word friends, see you soon!”

LESSON PLAN 12: ORAL LANGUAGE – FUN WITH TONGUE TWISTERS


I. OBJECTIVE

     At the end of the lesson, the pupils are expected to:

             1. Say simple tongue twisters clearly, focusing on sounds like

               /p/, /b/, and /s/.

             2. Practice saying tongue twisters slowly, then faster.
II. SUBJECT MATTER

     Topic: Tongue Twisters for Clear Speaking

      References: Grade 1 Phonics Activities

      Materials:

          Big posters with 3 tongue twisters (with pictures):

             1. “Peter Piper picked pickled peppers.” (Picture: Peter and

                  peppers)

             2. “Betty Botter bought butter.” (Picture: Betty and butter)

             3. “Six snails slide slowly.” (Picture: snails sliding)

         Sound cards with pictures (e.g., popcorn for /p/, ball for /b/,

           snake for /s/).

          “Tongue Twister Stars/Badge” stickers.

         Thumbs-up chart for group activities.
                                                           76


III. PROCEDURE
      1. Preparatory Activities

            A. Warm-Up (5 minutes):
                  Play “Copy the Sound!”:

                Teacher says: “/p/ like popping popcorn!” (Students

                mimic popping and say /p/).

               Repeat with /b/ (bounce like a ball) and /s/ (slither like a

                  snake).

            B. Motivation (3 minutes):

                 Say: “Let’s play with silly sentences that twist our

                  tongues! Who can say ‘Peter Piper’ fast without mixing up

                words?”

      2. Developmental Activities

            Introduce Tongue Twisters:

         Show the poster and read “Peter Piper” slowly. Clap for each

            word.

           Point to the /p/ sound card every time you say “p.”

          Say it faster like a robot! 🤖

          Group Practice:

           Repeat with “Betty Botter” (/b/ sound) and “Six snails” (/s/

               sound).

           Students take turns saying one line in pairs.
      3. Analysis/Discussion

           Ask:

         “Why is ‘Peter Piper’ tricky to say?” (They’ll say: “Too many /p/

              sounds!”).

        “How do tongue twisters help us?” (Answer: “They make our

           mouths strong for clear talking!”).
      4. Guided Practice

          Tongue Twister Game:

            In small groups, students pick a tongue twister.
                                                            77



          Say it slowly, then fast. Friends give a thumbs up if they hear

            the sounds clearly!

         Add fun: Hop or clap while saying it!


IV. EVALUATION

          Use a simple checklist:


     Give “Tongue Twister Star” stickers to everyone who tries!


 Criteria    🌟 (Great!)   👍 (Good!)       😊(Keep Trying!)

 Says sounds

 clearly

 Tries slow and

 fast

 Participates with

 a smile


V. AGREEMENT

           For homework:

      1. Practice one tongue twister with your family.

      2. Draw a picture of your favorite tongue twister (e.g., Peter Piper or

           snails).

assessments.title: Story Chain · pre-assessment
assessments.rubric:
LESSON 7: USING STORY CHAIN

    (Each student has their own story; pair up to tell it in first person, then switch

     pairs to retell the partner’s story)

    PRE-TEST (5 items)

    Assesses prior ability to tell a short story in first person.

     1. “Tell me a short story about something you did yesterday—start with ‘I’.”

     2. “Tell me a story about a time you played with a friend—use ‘I’ when talking

    about yourself.”

     3. “Tell me a short made-up story about a magical animal—start with ‘I saw a

    magical…’.”

     4. “Tell me a story about something that made you happy—use ‘I’.”

     5. “Tell me a short story about going to the park—start with ‘I went to the

    park…’.”

assessments.title: Story Chain · post-assessment
assessments.rubric:
LESSON 7: USING STORY CHAIN

(Each student has their own story; pair up to tell it in first person, then

switch pairs to retell the partner’s story)

POST-TEST (5 items)

Assesses ability to tell own story clearly and retell a partner’s story

Accurately.

(Setup: Give student a short made-up story to practice first, then pair with a

classmate)

1. “Tell your partner your story in first person—speak clearly so they can

hear all the details.”

2. “Now, retell your partner’s story to me—include at least two key details

(e.g., who was in it, what happened).”

3. “Tell your story again—make sure to start with ‘I’ and keep it in order.”

4. “Retell your partner’s story—use ‘he/she/they’ when talking about the

people in it.”

5. “Tell me one key detail from your partner’s story that you liked.”

assessments.title: Picture Talk · pre-assessment
assessments.rubric:
LESSON 8: USING PICTURE TALK
     Pre-Test

     1. Point to one thing in the picture and name it.

     2. What color is the [object] in the picture?

     3. Tell me about something big and/or small you see on the picture.

assessments.title: Picture Talk · post-assessment
assessments.rubric:
LESSON 8: USING PICTURE TALK

Post-Test
 1. Tell a short story (2-3 sentences) about the picture.

2. What might happen after the scene in the picture?

3. How would you feel if you were in this picture?

assessments.title: Recite, Clap & Smile · pre-assessment
assessments.rubric:
LESSON 9: USING POEMS

     Pre-test

     1. Clap the rhythm of a nursery rhyme (e.g., "Twinkle, Twinkle").

     2. Repeat a line from a simple poem after the teacher.

     3. Do you like poems that rhyme? Why?

assessments.title: Recite, Clap & Smile · post-assessment
assessments.rubric:
LESSON 9: USING POEMS

Post-Test

 1. Recite the entire poem with actions.

2. What is the poem mostly about? (Example: "It’s about rain.")

3. Draw a picture of your favorite part of the poem.

assessments.title: Talk, Play & Share · pre-assessment
assessments.rubric:
LESSON 10: TALK, PLAY AND SHARE

     Pre-Test

     1. Describe what the people or animals in the picture are doing.

    (Example: "The girl is jumping.")

     2. What do you think the weather is like in the picture? How do you know?

     3. Ask a friend: "What do you like about this picture?"

assessments.title: Talk, Play & Share · post-assessment
assessments.rubric:
LESSON 10: USING TALK, PLAY AND SHARE

Post-Test

1. Create a group story: Each student adds one sentence.

(Example: "Once, a dog met a cat...")

2. Act out a problem-solving scenario (e.g., sharing crayons).

3. Ask a friend: "What did you enjoy doing today?"

assessments.title: Word Friends · pre-assessment
assessments.rubric:
LESSON 11: USING WORD ASSOCIATION

    PRE-TEST (5 items)

    Assesses prior ability to think of one word related to a given word

     1. “I say ‘cat’—what’s one word that makes you think of ‘cat’?”

     2. “I say ‘sun’—what’s one word that goes with ‘sun’?”

     3. “I say ‘book’—what’s one word related to ‘book’?”

     4. “I say ‘water’—what’s one word that makes you think of ‘water’?”

     5. “I say ‘friend’—what’s one word that goes with ‘friend’?”

assessments.title: Word Friends · post-assessment
assessments.rubric:
LESSON 12: USING WORD ASOCIATION

POST-TEST (5 items)

Assesses ability to think of multiple related words and explain connections

1. “I say ‘dog’—tell me two words related to ‘dog’ and explain why (e.g., ‘bone’

because dogs like bones).”

2. “I say ‘school’—tell me three words that go with ‘school’.”

3. “I say ‘rain’—tell me two words related to ‘rain’ and say what they have to

do with rain.”

4. “I say ‘toy’—tell me three words that make you think of ‘toy’.”

5. “I say ‘food’—tell me two words related to ‘food’ and explain why.”

activities.prompt: 39 LESSON PLAN 1: ORAL LANGUAGE – TALKING ABOUT ONESELF AND ONE’S FAMILY I. OBJECTIVES At the end of the 45-minute lesson, the students will be able to: 1. Share at least 3 key details about oneself (name, age, favorite activity) using clear voice and proper pronunciation; 2. Talk about 2-3 family members and one thing they like to do together; 3. Maintain eye contact with their audience when speaking. II. SUBJECT MATTER Topic: Sharing Information About Oneself and One’s Family References: Adapted from elementary oral communication curricula and early childhood language development resources Materials: Visual aid (chart) with sentence starters: "My name is…", "I am years old…", "My family has…", "We like to…" Picture cards (e.g., of a child, parents, siblings, toys, activities like playing, eating) "About Me" worksheet (simple, with spaces for drawing and writing key details) Evaluation checklist III. PROCEDURE 1. PREPARATORY ACTIVITIES Warm-Up Lead a "Hello Circle" – students stand in a circle, take turns saying "Hello, my name is [name]" while waving to the class. Encourage them to speak loudly enough for everyone to hear. 40 Motivation Show a colorful picture of a happy family doing an activity (e.g., picnicking). Ask: "Who do you see in this picture?" and "What do you like to do with your own family?" Let 2-3 students share a quick thought to get them excited to talk more. 2. DEVELOPMENTAL ACTIVITIES Introduce Key Details: Display the visual aid with sentence starters. Explain that when we talk about ourselves and our family, we can use these sentences to make our ideas clear. Modeling: Share your own example in simple terms: "Hi, my name is [Teacher’s Name]. I am [age]. My favorite activity is reading. My family has [2 people] – my mom and dad. We like to cook together on weekends!" Use picture cards to point to each detail as you speak. Practice Sentence Starters: Have the class repeat the sentence starters together 2-3 times to build confidence. 3. GUIDED PRACTICE Pair-and-Share Activity: Divide students into pairs. Give each pair a set of picture cards to use as clues. 1. Student A uses the sentence starters to share about themselves and their family. 41 2. Student B listens, then shares their own information. 3. Circulate around pairs to support: remind them to speak clearly, make eye contact, and use the picture cards if they get stuck. After 8 minutes, ask 2-3 volunteer pairs to share one thing they learned about each other with the class. IV. EVALUATION Use an informal checklist to assess each student during pair-and-share: 1 2 3 4 Pupil mentioned Pupil mentioned Pupil mentioned Pupil mentioned only his name 2 – 3 details 4 details about 5 or more details about himself himself about himself V. AGREEMENT For homework, students will: Talk to one family member about their favorite activity. Draw a picture of themselves and that family member doing that activity. Be ready to share what they learned with the class in our next lesson.

Listen carefully to follow 1-step and 2-step oral directions accurately; 2. Repeat the directions in their own words before completing them; 3. Perform the actions in the correct order. II. PREPARATORY ACTIVITIES Warm-Up (5 minutes): Lead the class in an "Action Song" (e.g., "Head, Shoulders, Knees, and Toes") – have them follow along with your oral cues to practice listening and moving. DEVELOPMENTAL ACTIVITIES Introduce 1-Step Directions: Display the visual aid with action words. Give a simple 1-step direction (e.g., "Go to the chair") and do it yourself to model. activities.prompt: LESSON PLAN 3: ORAL LANGUAGE – GIVING AND FOLLOWING 1-TO-2- STEP ORAL DIRECTIONS IN DAILY SITUATIONS I. OBJECTIVE At the end of the 45-minute lesson, the students will be able to: 1. Give clear 1-2 step oral directions using polite language (e.g., "can you," "please"); 2. Follow 1-2 step directions given by a peer; 3. Identify 2 key elements of effective directions (clarity, order) and polite communication. II. SUBJECT MATTER Topic: Giving and Following 1-2-Step Directions (e.g., Asking a Sibling to Tidy Up Toys) References: Adapted from elementary oral communication curricula and social skills development resources 45 Materials: Visual aid (chart) with: Polite phrase starters: "Can you…?", "Please…", "Thank you!" Action words with pictures: keep away, put in, pick up, close Toy props (dolls, cars, blocks, a toy box) Scenario cards (e.g., "Your younger sister left toys on the floor", "Your brother left books on the couch") Informal evaluation checklist III. PROCEDURE 1. PREPARATORY ACTIVITIES Warm-Up (5 minutes): Lead a "Follow My Lead" game: Give 1-2 step directions (e.g., "Pick up one block and put it on your desk") and have the class do them together. This review following directions before moving to giving them. Motivation (5 minutes): Show a photo of a messy playroom with toys scattered. Ask: "Have you ever seen a room like this? If your younger sister made this mess, what would you say to ask her to clean it up?" Let 2-3 students share quick ideas, then say: "Today, we’ll learn to ask nicely with clear steps so she knows exactly what to do!" 2. DEVELOPMENTAL ACTIVITIES (15 minutes) Introduce Polite Directions: Display the visual aid with polite phrases. Explain that when asking someone to do something, we use kind words like "can you" and "please" to be respectful. 46 Model Giving 2-Step Directions: Use the toy props to act out the scenario: "Let’s pretend this doll is my younger sister, and these toys are on the floor. I’ll say: “‘Can you please keep your toys away and put them in the toy box?’" Point to the action pictures ("keep away," "put in") as you speak to show order. Practice Making Directions: Have the class repeat the model direction together. Then, guide them to make their own 2-step direction for the same scenario (e.g., "Can you pick up your cars and put them on the shelf?"). 3. ANALYSIS / DISCUSSION Ask: "What polite words did I use when asking my sister?" (Let students point to the visual aid.) Follow up: "What was the first step I asked her to do? The second step? Why is order important?" (e.g., "So, she doesn’t get confused," "So, she does everything needed"). Ask: "How do you think your sister would feel if you asked nicely vs. yelling?" (Emphasize that polite language helps others want to help.) 4. GUIDED PRACTICE Role-Play Activity: Divide students into pairs. Give each pair a scenario card and toy props. 1. One student plays the "older sibling" and gives a clear 2-step direction using polite language. 2. The other student plays the "younger sibling," listens, and follows the directions. 3. Pairs switch roles after 5 minutes. 47 Circulate around pairs to support: Remind them to use polite phrases, keep directions clear, and follow steps in order. Example scenario prompt for pairs: "Your younger sister left her dolls on the bed. What 2 things will you ask her to do?" IV. EVALUATION Use an informal checklist to assess each student during the role-play: Uses polite Gives clear Listens language (can 2-step directions carefully and Criteria you, please) in the correct follows peer’s when giving order directions directions accurately Excellent Good Satisfactory Note: Assess by observing each pair once. Give positive feedback like, "Great job asking nicely!" or "Perfect order of steps!" V. AGREEMENT For homework, students will: Find a time to give one 2-step direction to a family member (sibling, parent, or grandparent) using polite language (e.g., "Can you please pass the spoon and put it on my plate?"). Ask the family member if they understood the directions. Share what direction they gave and how it went with the class in our next lesson.

activities.prompt: 48 LESSON PLAN 4: ORAL LANGUAGE – USING DESCRIBING WORDS FOR PEOPLE, OBJECTS, THINGS, AND PLACES I. OBJECTIVE At the end of the 45-minute lesson, the students will be able to: 1. Use describing words to talk about people, objects, things, and places. (color, shape, size, height, weight, length, distance, etc.) 2. Match describing words to the attributes of what they are talking about. II. SUBJECT MATTER Topic: Recognizing and Using Describing Words (Attributes: Color, Shape, Size, Height, Weight, Length, Distance) References: Adapted from elementary oral language curricula and vocabulary development resources Materials: Visual aid (chart) titled "My Describing Word Toolkit" – with words and pictures: red, round, big, tall, heavy, long, far, cozy Props with different attributes: colored blocks, toys (ball, box, car, doll), books (thick, thin), plants (tall, short), photos of places (sunny park, quiet room) "Describe It!" cards (with pictures of people, objects, or places) Informal evaluation checklist III. PROCEDURE 1. PREPARATORY ACTIVITIES Warm-Up (5 minutes): Lead a "Word Clue" game: Say, "I’m thinking of something in this room that’s red. Can you guess what it is?" Have students call out guesses, then reveal the object. Repeat with 3-4 more clues (e.g., "It’s round," "It’s big"). 49 Motivation (5 minutes): Show a plain drawing of a cat and a colorful, detailed drawing of the same cat. Ask: "Which drawing tells you more about the cat? Why?" Explain: "Today, we’ll learn about ‘describing words’ – these are like magic clues that help us tell others exactly what something looks like, feels like, or where it is!" 2. DEVELOPMENTAL ACTIVITIES Introduce Describing Words: Display the "Describing Word Toolkit" chart. Point to each word and its picture, and say: "These words describe attributes – what something is like. ‘Red’ is a color, ‘round’ is a shape, ‘big’ is a size, and ‘far’ is a distance." Have students repeat each word aloud. Describing words toolkit (see intervention materials) 1. Colors Red, blue, green, yellow, orange, purple, pink, black, white, brown 2. Sizes Big, small, tall, short, long, tiny, huge 3. Shapes Round, square, triangle, circle, flat 50 4. How things feel Soft, hard, smooth, rough, sticky, fuzzy, warm, cold 5. How things look Bright, dark, shiny, dull, clean, dirty, wet, dry 6. Feelings (for people/animals) Happy, sad, angry, scared, excited, sleepy, friendly 7. Numbers (to describe how many) One, two, three, many, few, some Model Using Describing Words: Pick up a red, round ball and say: "This is a red, round ball. It’s also small enough to hold in my hand." Then point to a tall plant: "This is a tall, green plant that’s near the window." Model for a person too: "My friend Lila has curly, brown hair and she is happy today." Practice Naming Attributes: Hold up different props (e.g., thick book, heavy toy car) and ask: "What describing words can we use for this?" Have students share ideas and match them to the chart. 3. ANALYSIS / DISCUSSION Ask: "Why do we use describing words when we talk?" (Let students share: "So others can picture what we’re talking about," "To be clear," "To make stories more fun"). Follow up: "Can we use more than one describing word for something? Let’s try with the box – is it square, blue, or both?" (Emphasize that we can combine words to give more details). Ask: "What describing words can we use for places, like a park?" (e.g., "sunny," "big," "busy"). 51 4. GUIDED PRACTICE "Describe It! Share It!" Activity: Divide students into pairs. Give each pair a "Describe It!" card with a picture (e.g., a cozy bedroom, a small yellow bird, a tall boy). 1. One student looks at the picture and thinks of 2-3 describing words for it. 2. They say the describing words aloud (e.g., "It’s cozy, quiet, and has a big bed") and their partner guesses what’s in the picture. 3. Pairs switch roles after 5 minutes. Circulate to support: Remind students to use words from the toolkit and match them to the picture’s attributes. IV. EVALUATION Use an informal checklist to assess each student during the pair activity: Recognizes Uses describing Matches and names at words to talk about describing Criteria least 4 people/objects/places words to the describing correct words attributes Excellent Good Satisfactory Note: Assess by listening to each pair’s descriptions. Give positive feedback like, "Great use of ‘cozy’ for the bedroom!" or "Perfect – ‘tall’ matches the boy!" V. AGREEMENT For homework, students will: 1. Pick one thing at home (a toy, a pet, a room) and think of 3 describing words for it. 2. Tell a family member about it using those words (e.g., "My dog is brown, fluffy, and small"). Be ready to share their description with the class in our next lesson.

activities.prompt: 52 LESSON PLAN 5: ORAL LANGUAGE – TALKING ABOUT TOPICS OF INTEREST THROUGH PICTURE DISCUSSION I. OBJECTIVE At the end of the 45-minute lesson, the students will be able to: 1. Share their thoughts, feelings, and observations about a picture on a topic of interest; 2. Use simple sentence starters to organize their ideas clearly; 3. Listen respectfully to peers’ thoughts and ask one follow-up question. II. SUBJECT MATTER Topic: Talking About Topics of Interest (e.g., Toys, Pets, Parks, Festivals) "Tell Me What You Think About This Picture" References: Adapted from elementary oral communication curricula and expressive language development resources Materials: Visual aid (chart) with sentence starters: "I see…", "I think…", "I like…", "It makes me feel…" Colorful pictures of kid-friendly topics (e.g., a dog playing in a park, a birthday party with toys, a colorful festival, a cozy pet corner) "Picture Card Packs" (one pack per small group, with 3-4 pictures on different interests) informal evaluation checklist. 1. PREPARATORY ACTIVITIES Warm-Up Lead a "Quick Share" circle: Ask students to say one sentence about something they love (e.g., "I love my cat" or "I love playing with blocks"). Encourage them to speak clearly and look at the class. valuation checklist 53 Motivation Hold up a bright picture of a dog playing in a sunny park. Ask: "Who likes dogs? What do you see in this picture? What do you think the dog is feeling?" Let 2-3 students call out quick ideas, then say: "Today, we’ll learn to share our thoughts about pictures we like – and hear what our friends think too!" 2. DEVELOPMENTAL ACTIVITIES Introduce Picture Discussion: Display the visual aid with sentence starters. Explain: "When we talk about a picture, these sentences help us share what’s in our minds clearly. ‘I see’ tells what’s in the picture, ‘I think’ tells our ideas, and ‘I like’ tells what we enjoy about it." Model Sharing Thoughts: Focus on the dog park picture and share your own ideas: "I see a brown dog running with a red ball. I think the dog is happy because it’s playing in the sun. I like this picture because it makes me want to go to the park too!" Point to each sentence starter on the chart as you speak. Practice Sentence Starters: Have the class repeat the sentence starters together. Then, guide them to share one thought about the dog picture using one of the starters (e.g., "I see green grass" or "It makes me feel happy"). 3. ANALYSIS / DISCUSSION Ask: "What did I do to help you understand my thoughts about the picture?" (Let students point to the sentence starters.) Follow up: "Why is it fun to talk about pictures we like?" (e.g., "Because we can share what we love," "We can learn what our friends like too"). Remind them: "When others are talking, we listen carefully – that’s how we show we care about their ideas. We can even ask a small question, like ‘Why do you like that?’ to learn more!" 54 4. GUIDED PRACTICE "Picture Talk" Groups: Divide students into small groups (4-5 students each) and give each group a "Picture Card Pack" with topics they’ll enjoy. 1. One student picks a picture from the pack and shares their thoughts using at least 2 sentence starters. 2. The other students listen, then one peer asks a follow-up question (e.g., "What do you think the cat in the picture is eating?"). 3. Everyone in the group takes a turn picking a picture and sharing. Circulate around groups to support: Remind them to use the sentence starters, speak clearly, and listen respectfully. III. EVALUATION Use an informal checklist to assess each student during group discussion: Shares Uses at least 2 Listens thoughts/observations sentence respectfully to Criteria about the picture starters to peers and asks organize ideas a follow-up question Excellent Good Satisfactory Note: Assess by observing each student’s participation. Give positive feedback like, "Great use of ‘I think’!" or "Nice question – that helped us learn more!" IV. AGREEMENT For homework, students will: 1. - Find a picture at home (in a book, on a calendar, or on a device with family help) of something they love. 2. - Talk to a family member about it using the sentence starters: "I see…", "I think…", "I like…". Be ready to share their picture and thoughts with the class in our next lesson.

30 "This game works best with a small to medium-sized group of people, so that everyone gets a chance to ask a question. Choose a random player to be “it.” This could be the youngest player in the group, the player who’s had the most recent birthday, or something silly, like who can eat a piece of pizza the fastest. Question 1 Think of a person, place, or thing for other players to guess if you’re “it. ”Think of someone or something that you know enough about to answer some basic questions about, and keep it a secret! If you choose a person, they can be living, deceased, or even fictional. Make sure you choose a person, place, or thing that most people in your group know about. • For example, your item could be “Manny Pacquiao,” since he is famous enough that most people will be able to make guesses about him. You could also choose something like your town, Philippines, or even clouds or the sun. • Avoid items like “my mom” or “my dog” unless you are with your siblings or best friends, since the players might not know enough about them to guess. Question 2 Ask yes-or-no questions if you're not "it. "If you’re not “it,” your goal is to figure out what the “it” person is thinking of by asking questions to narrow down the possibilities. Try using a fairly general opening question that can be answered with “yes” or “no” to narrow down your options.

31 For example: • “Is it alive?” • “Is it an object?” • “Is it fictional?” • “Is it bigger than a toaster? Question 3 Take turns asking more specific yes-or-no questions to narrow it down. You can ask questions in any order that you’d like, but make sure each player gets to ask at least 1 question. If a player asks a question that can’t be answered with “yes” or “no,” ask them to rephrase it so that it can be, since the person who’s “it” can only say “yes” or “no.” • For example, a player couldn’t ask, “How old are they?” or “What do they look like?” They could ask, “Are they older than 50?” or, “Do they have blonde hair?” Think about the questions that have already been asked before you ask new questions. For example, you could go from "Is it a person?" to "Is it a man?" to "Are they alive?" to "Do they live in the Philippines?" Play until you reach 10 questions or someone guesses the right answer. Become the next “it” person if you guess the correct answer. The person who guesses the right answer is next to be “it,” and they think up their own secret person, place, or thing. If no one guessed the person, place, or thing at all, whoever wants to go next can have a turn. Keep the game going until everyone has had a chance to be “it.” • If someone guesses correctly but they’ve already been “it,” let someone else have a turn instead. Giving everyone a turn makes the game more inclusive and lets everybody have some fun!

activities.prompt: 55 LESSON PLAN 6: ORAL LANGUAGE – DESCRIBE AND DRAW I. OBJECTIVE At the end of the 45-minute lesson, the students will be able to: 1. Use specific describing words (color, shape, size, position) to clearly describe a picture; 2. Listen carefully to a peer’s description and draw what they hear; 3. Identify 2-3 key details that make a description easy to understand. II. SUBJECT MATTER Topic: "Describe and Draw" – Using Oral Language to Share Visual Details References: Adapted from elementary oral communication curricula and expressive/receptive language development resources Materials: Teacher’s model picture (colorful, with clear details: e.g., a red bird on a green tree branch next to a yellow flower) Set of "secret pictures" (one per pair, different from each other, with simple, distinct elements) Paper and crayons for each student Visual aid (chart) with key describing words: color words, round, square, big, small, on top, next to, under Informal evaluation checklist III. PROCEDURE 1. PREPARATORY ACTIVITIES Warm-Up Lead a "Quick Draw" game: Say, "I’m going to describe something—draw what you hear!" Describe a simple object (e.g., "a small, blue square") and have students draw it. Show their drawings and talk about how clear words helped them. Motivation Hold up your model picture (but don’t show it to the class yet). Say: "I have a secret picture! If I describe it well enough, you’ll be able to draw it without even seeing it. Want to try? Today, we’ll play a ‘Describe and Draw’ game where we’re like ‘picture messengers’—using words to send images to our friends!" 56 2. DEVELOPMENTAL ACTIVITIES Introduce Key Description Details: Display the visual aid. Explain: "When we describe a picture, we need to share details like what color things are, what shape they are, how big they are, and where they are. These details help the person drawing know exactly what to put on their paper." Teacher Modeling: Show the model picture to the class for 10 seconds, then hide it. Describe it slowly and clearly: "First, there’s a big, green tree branch in the middle. On top of the branch, there’s a small, red bird with a yellow beak. Next to the bird, there’s a bright yellow flower with five petals. The sky behind is light blue." As you describe, point to the words on the visual aid. Have students draw along as you speak. Check and Discuss: Show the model picture again and let students compare their drawings. Ask: "What details helped you draw it right?" (e.g., "‘on top’ told me where the bird was," "‘red’ told me its color"). 3. ANALYSIS / DISCUSSION Ask: "What would happen if I forgot to say ‘small’ about the bird? Or ‘next to the bird’ about the flower?" (Let students share: "I might draw a big bird," "I might put the flower somewhere else"). Follow up: "Why is it important to describe things in order (e.g., ‘first the branch, then the bird’)?" (e.g., "So the drawer knows what to draw first," "It’s easier to follow"). Remind students: "As a describer, your job is to be clear. As a drawer, your job is to listen closely—no peeking at the picture!" 4. GUIDED PRACTICE Pair "Describe and Draw" Activity: Divide students into pairs. Give one student in each pair a "secret picture" (they must not show it 57 to their partner). Assign roles: Describer (has the picture) and Drawer (listens and draws). 1. The Describer looks at their picture and describes it using key details and the visual aid words. 2. The Drawer listens carefully and draws what they hear—they can ask clarifying questions (e.g., "Is the cat big or small?"). 3. After 5 minutes, have pairs switch roles with a new secret picture. Circulate around pairs to support: Remind Describers to use specific details and Drawers to listen actively. IV. EVALUATION Use an informal checklist to assess each student in both roles Uses specific Captures key Listens Criteria describing words details from the respectfully and (color, shape, description asks clarifying position) As Drawer questions (when As Describer drawing) Excellent Good Satisfactory Note: Assess by observing pairs and looking at their drawings. Give positive feedback like, "Great job saying ‘under the tree’—that helped your partner draw it right!" V. AGREEMENT For homework, students will: 1. Pick a favorite toy at home (e.g., a doll, car, teddy bear). 2. Describe the toy in detail to a family member, who will draw it based on their description. 3. Bring both the toy and the family’s drawing to share with the class in our next lesson.

activities.prompt: 58 LESSON PLAN 7: ORAL LANGUAGE USING PICTURE STORY CHAIN STRATEGY I. OBJECTIVES By the end of the lesson, students will be able to: 1. Identify key elements (characters, setting, action) in a sequence of pictures. 2. Contribute at least one sentence to a group "picture story chain." 3. Speak clearly and listen attentively when participating in the group activity. II. SUBJECT MATTER Topic: Oral Language Development through Picture Story Chain Strategy: Picture Story Chain (collaborative storytelling using a sequence of images) Materials: 5-6 colorful, simple picture cards (no text) showing a logical sequence (e.g., a cat waking up → going outside → finding a ball → playing with it → going home → sleeping again) Whiteboard or chart paper Marker Sticky notes for student contributions Skills: Speaking, listening, sequencing, critical thinking Values Integration: Cooperation, respect for others’ ideas III. LEARNING PROCEDURE A. MOTIVATION "Guess the Next Picture" Game: Show the first 2 picture cards one by one. Ask: "What do you see in this picture? What do you think will happen next?" Let 2-3 students share their guesses to activate prior knowledge and spark curiosity. 59 B. LESSON PROPER 1. INTRODUCTION TO PICTURE STORY CHAIN Show all 4-5 picture cards in order on the board. Explain: “Today, we’ll make a story together using these pictures! This is called a 'Picture Story Chain.' Each of you will add one sentence to the story, just like linking chains together." Point to each picture and ask students to name what they see (e.g., "This is a cat. This is a garden. This is a ball.") to build vocabulary. 2. MODELING THE ACTIVITY Start the story with the first picture: "Once upon a time, there was a little cat named Mimi. She woke up early in her cozy bed." Move to the second picture and add: "Mimi jumped out of bed and walked outside to the garden. Write these sentences on the chart paper to show how the story builds. Emphasize: "Each sentence should connect to the picture and the one before it!" 60 3. GROUP PICTURE STORY CHAIN Divide the class into 5 small groups (4-5 students each). Group 1 Group 2 61 Group 3 Group 4 62 Group 5 Give each group a set of the picture cards arranged in order. Instructions for groups: • The first student looks at the first picture and says one sentence. • The next student looks at the second picture and says a sentence that connects to the first. • Continue until all pictures are used and the story has an ending. • One student from each group will share the complete story with the class. Roam around groups to support: Encourage shy students to participate (e.g., "Can you say, 'Mimi found a red ball'?") Help students connect their sentences (e.g., "Great! After Mimi plays with the ball, what happens next?") Write key sentences on sticky notes for each group to display. C. GENERALIZATION Gather the class and have both groups share their stories. Ask: "How did working together help us make the story?" (Expected answer: "We shared ideas, listened to each other, and made a long story together.") Conclude: "Pictures can help us tell stories, and when we work in a chain, we can make amazing stories with our friends!" 63 IV. EVALUATION Formative Assessment: Observe students during the group activity and check if they: Contribute at least one sentence. Speak clearly. Listen to others. Use a simple checklist to record participation and understanding. V. ASSIGNMENT At home, ask students to find 3 simple pictures (from a book or magazine) and make a short story with their family using the picture story chain strategy. They will share their story with the class in the next lesson. VI. REFLECTION (For teacher’s use only: Note which students struggled with speaking/listening, which pictures were most effective, and adjustments for future lessons.) Picture Card Suggestion (Description for Visuals): 1. A small cat lying in a bed with eyes closed. 2. The cat standing by an open door, looking outside. 3. The cat in a garden with green grass and flowers. 4. The cat playing with a red ball. 5. The cat walking back towards the house with the ball. 6. The cat back in bed, sleeping with the ball beside it.
